content:
### The Measurement Problem With Territory Programs

Every corporate marketing director who evaluates SIT™ programs eventually asks the same question: how do we measure it?

It is the right question — and the honest answer is that standard marketing metrics are not designed to capture what territory presence produces. CPL (cost per lead), ROAS (return on ad spend), CTR (click-through rate) — these metrics were built to measure campaign outputs. Territory presence does not produce campaign outputs. It produces something different and more valuable: recognition equity.

### What Recognition Equity Is

Recognition equity is the accumulated value of homeowner familiarity with a brand in a specific geographic area. It is not a lead. It is not a conversion. It is a compound asset — one that grows with every neighborhood interaction and depreciates very slowly once built.

A roofing company with twelvemonths of SIT GroundForce™ territory presence in Winnetka has recognition equity in that market. Homeowners in the target neighborhoods know the brand —not because they have been advertised to, but because they have experienced consistent, repeated presence. That recognition converts to calls, referrals, and repeat business at rates that no standard metric is designed to capture.

### Why Standard Metrics Undervalue Territory Programs

A digital advertising campaign that generates 40 leads at $50 CPL produces a clear, measurable output that finance teams and marketing directors can evaluate easily. A territory presence program that generates 8 leads in the same period — but where those 8 leads convert at 60% rather than 12%, and where 6 of them become recurring annual customers, and where 4 of them generate referrals within the first year —produces a superior return that the initial CPL comparison completely obscures.

The measurement framework for territory programs requires a longer evaluation window and different success metrics: conversion rate from first contact, average customer lifetime value within the territory, referral generation rate, and year-over-year recognition increase in the target geography.

### How to Evaluate a Territory Program Correctly

The three metrics that actually capture territory program value are: conversion rate from awareness to first contact (how many homeowners who recognized the brand converted to an inquiry),lifetime value of territory-acquired customers versus digitally-acquired customers, and recognition rate increase over time in the target geography.

These metrics require patience —they are measured in quarters and years, not days and weeks. But they are the metrics that correlate with the kind of market dominance that standard campaign metrics never produce.

### The Compound Advantage in Measurable Terms

The most honest framing of territory presence ROI is this: a 12-month territory program investment that produces $X in direct revenue in year one typically produces $2X to $3X in year two from the same territory — because recognition equity compounds, referral networks activate, and the brand becomes the default choice for homeowners who were simply not yet ready in year one.

No digital campaign produces that compounding dynamic. Territory infrastructure does.
